statement: In a class, 60% of the pupils are girls and the rest are boys. 25% of the girls and 50% of the boys walk to school. What percentage of the whole class walks to school?

choices.misconception: I only counted the girls who walk, 25% of 60%, and forgot the boys.
I averaged 25% and 50%, but there are more girls than boys, so the two groups do not count equally.
I mixed up the groups and took 50% of the girls and 25% of the boys.
I added 25% and 50%, but those are percentages of two different groups.

hints: Imagine that the class has 100 pupils.
Percentages of different groups cannot simply be added or averaged. Turn each group into a number of pupils out of 100, find the walkers in each group, then add those numbers.
With 100 pupils there are 60 girls and 40 boys. A quarter of 60 is 15.

solutions.reliable: Imagine 100 pupils: 60 girls and 40 boys. 25% of the 60 girls is 15 girls, and 50% of the 40 boys is 20 boys. So 35 of the 100 pupils walk, which is 35%. The transferable idea: percentages of different groups must be turned into amounts of one whole before you combine them.

whyOnTest: Percentages of different-sized groups are a classic trap: they cannot be added or averaged, only turned into counts of one whole.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
